questions.q: The chapter opens myelopathy with which definition?
opts: Cortical sensory loss with normal reflexes
Sensory, motor or ANS symptoms d/t disease of spinal cord
Radicular pain alone, without long-tract signs
Lower-motor-neuron weakness from anterior horn cell loss alone
questions.exp: myelopathy : Sensory, motor or ANS symptoms d/t disease of spinal cord (Book p660)

questions.q: The first printed division of myelopathy is into:
questions.exp: Types : Compressive, Non-compressive (Book p660)

questions.q: Compressive myelopathy is introduced with which temporal profile?
questions.exp: Compressive Myelopathy : Chronic course (Book p660)

questions.q: In the printed flowchart, compressive myelopathy first branches into:
questions.exp: Flowchart : Compressive myelopathy → Intramedullary / Extramedullary (Book p660)

questions.q: The extramedullary branch is subdivided into which two columns?
questions.exp: Extramedullary → Intradural : / Extradural (m/c) (Book p660)

questions.q: Which compartment is explicitly tagged (m/c) for compressive myelopathy?
questions.exp: Extradural (m/c) (Book p660)

questions.q: Which tumour is NOT listed in the intramedullary column?
questions.exp: Intramedullary tumors : Ependymoma, Oligodendroglioma, medulloblastoma (meningioma appears under Intradural) (Book p660)

questions.q: The intramedullary column's 'expansion of cavity' cause is:
questions.exp: Expansion of cavity : Syringomyelia (Book p660)

questions.q: The four intradural causes printed are:
opts: Neurofibroma, meningioma, arachnoid cyst and pachymeningitis
questions.exp: Intradural Cause : Neurofibroma, meningioma, Arachnoid cyst, Pachymeningitis (Book p660)

questions.q: Under extradural 'lesion of vertebrae', the infections printed are:
questions.exp: Lesion of vertebrae - Infection : Te (TB), syphilis (Book p660)

questions.q: Also listed under extradural vertebral lesions, besides fracture and infection, is:
questions.exp: Pyogenic abscess (Book p660)

questions.q: The metastatic primaries named for extradural vertebral lesions are:
questions.exp: metastasis (Prostate & ovary Ca) (Book p660)

questions.q: The disc lesion tagged (m/c) in the extradural column is:
opts: Spinal stenosis from ligamentum flavum hypertrophy
questions.exp: Disc pathology : IVDP (m/c) (Book p660)

questions.q: Which vascular lesion completes the extradural list?
questions.exp: Aneurysm of aorta (Book p660)

questions.q: A 63-year-old man treated for prostate carcinoma develops three months of progressive spastic legs with a T10 sensory level. On this page's classification, where does the compression sit?
questions.exp: Extradural (m/c) - Lesion of vertebrae : metastasis (Prostate & ovary Ca); chronic course fits compressive myelopathy (Book p660)

questions.q: The axial canal diagram labels which combination of layers and spaces?
opts: Dura mater, epidural space, subarachnoid space and arachnoid membrane
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments only
questions.exp: Figure labels : Dura mater; Epidural space; Subarachnoid space; Arachnoid membrane; Extradural tumor (Book p660)

questions.q: The three lower schematic columns are captioned in printed order as:
opts: Ventral, central and dorsal cord compression
questions.exp: Bottom row captions : Extradural extramedullary; Intradural extramedullary; Intramedullary (Book p660)

questions.q: The three sagittal MRI panels a-c carry which caption?
questions.exp: MRI panel caption : Tumors of spinal cord (Book p660)

questions.q: The single sagittal MRI at the bottom right is labelled:
questions.exp: Bottom-right image label : IVDP (Book p660)

questions.q: The back pain of compressive myelopathy is described as:
questions.exp: Chronic back pain : moderate to severe intensity (Book p661)

questions.q: The printed reason pain is worse on erect posture is:
questions.exp: worse on erect posture : (Neurogenic claudication : Canal diameter ↓ in standing/erect position) (Book p661)

questions.q: Which posture relieves this pain, as printed?
questions.exp: Relief on bending (Cycling) (Book p661)

questions.q: The brace beside the erect-posture and bending entries labels them as:
questions.exp: Bracket : Definitive symptoms of compression (Book p661)

questions.q: Tingling, numbness and paresthesia in these patients are usually:
opts: On both lower limbs bilaterally, depending on level
questions.exp: Tingling, numbness, paresthesia : Usually on both lower limbs (LL) bilaterally depending on level (Book p661)

questions.q: The band-like sensation at the level of involvement is printed as:
questions.exp: Band like sensation (Hyperesthesia) at the level of involvement (Book p661)

questions.q: The printed example of a band-like sensation at the umbilicus corresponds to which level?
questions.exp: Eg : Umbilicus if T10 level is involved (Book p661)

questions.q: In the neurogenic-vascular claudication table, walking distance is:
opts: Fixed in neurogenic, variable in vascular
Variable in neurogenic, fixed in vascular
questions.exp: Note table : Walking distance — Neurogenic variable; Vascular fixed (Book p661)

questions.q: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by:
questions.exp: Relieved on — Neurogenic : Sitting/bending; Vascular : Standing (Book p661)

questions.q: Vascular claudication is worsened specifically by:
questions.exp: Worsened on — Neurogenic : Walking/standing (erect posture); Vascular : walking (Book p661)

questions.q: Walking uphill is painful in vascular claudication; for neurogenic claudication the table prints it as:
questions.exp: Walking uphill — Neurogenic : Painless; Vascular : Painful (Book p661)

questions.q: A diabetic man gets calf pain after a fixed distance of walking which is relieved by standing still; pedal pulses are absent. Which column of this table fits him?
questions.exp: Vascular claudication : fixed distance, relieved on standing, pulse absent, painful uphill, bicycle test positive (Painful) (Book p661)

questions.q: The bicycle test rows read:
opts: Negative in neurogenic, positive (painful) in vascular
Positive in neurogenic, negative in vascular
questions.exp: Bicycle test — Neurogenic : Negative; Vascular : Positive (Painful) (Book p661)

questions.q: Which finding points to vascular rather than neurogenic claudication?
questions.exp: Pulse : Absent in vascular claudication (Present in neurogenic) (Book p661)

questions.q: Weakness on the two rows of the table is printed as:
opts: Occasionally in neurogenic, rarely in vascular
Rarely in neurogenic, occasionally in vascular
questions.exp: Weakness — Neurogenic : Occasionally; Vascular : Rarely (Book p661)

questions.q: Back pain frequency across the table is:
opts: Occasionally in neurogenic, commonly in vascular
Commonly in neurogenic, occasionally in vascular
questions.exp: Back pain — Neurogenic : Commonly; Vascular : Occasionally (Book p661)

questions.q: The pain-character row prints neurogenic pain as:
opts: Numbness and aching, proximal to distal
questions.exp: Pain character — Neurogenic : Numbness, aching, proximal to distal (Book p661)

questions.q: Vascular pain character in the same row is:
opts: Numbness and aching, proximal to distal
questions.exp: Pain character — Vascular : Cramping : Distal to proximal (Book p661)

questions.q: A clerk reports bilateral leg numbness after standing in a queue, relieved by squatting, with normal pedal pulses and no pain on cycling. The mechanism printed for his symptoms is:
opts: Canal diameter falls in the erect posture
questions.exp: Neurogenic claudication : Canal diameter ↓ in standing/erect position; relieved on bending, bicycle test negative, pulse present (Book p661)

questions.q: In the examination list, higher mental function and cranial nerves are:
questions.exp: Examination findings : Higher mental function (HMF), cranial nerves (CN) : Normal (Book p661)

questions.q: With compression below T1, upper-limb motor power is:
questions.exp: motor : Upper limb : Compression below T1 → Power intact (S/S) (Book p661)

questions.q: Lower-limb motor findings in compressive myelopathy are:
opts: Reduced power with B/L UMN features
Reduced power with B/L LMN features
Normal power with sensory loss only
questions.exp: Lower limb : Reduced power; B/L UMN features (Book p661)

questions.q: Which pair of sensory pathways is printed as lost in the lower limbs?
questions.exp: Sensory Lower limb : Spinothalamic tract loss + Posterior column loss → Loss (Book p661)

questions.q: Reflex findings in the lower limbs are:
opts: Absent knee jerk, brisk ankle jerk
Exaggerated knee jerk and ankle jerk
questions.exp: Reflexes : Lower limb : Exaggerated (Knee jerk, ankle jerk) (Book p661)

questions.q: Bowel and bladder involvement is tied to which pattern?
questions.exp: Bowel & bladder involvement : In intramedullary compression (Book p661)

questions.q: LMN findings, wasting, band-like sensation, hyperesthesia, hypesthesia and hypoalgesia are printed as occurring:
questions.exp: Level localization : LMN findings, wasting atrophy, band like sensation, hyperesthesia, hypesthesia, hypoalgesia : At the level of lesion (Book p662)

questions.q: UMN findings appear below the lesion, with which reflex pattern?
opts: Superficial reflexes lost, deep reflexes exaggerated
Both superficial and deep reflexes lost
questions.exp: UMN findings : Below the level of lesion (Superficial reflexes lost, deep reflexes exaggerated) (Book p662)

questions.q: A normal upper limb indicates the lesion lies:
opts: Below T1, with levels above the involvement spared
questions.exp: upper limb normal : Lesion below T1 (Above level of involvement : Spared) (Book p662)

questions.q: Sensory symptoms plus weakness in both lower limbs are bracketed as a lesion:
questions.exp: Sensory symptoms in both lower limb + weakness of both lower limb → Lesion above L1 spinal segment (Book p662)

questions.q: A positive Beevor's sign localises the lesion:
questions.exp: Beevor's sign positive : Lesion below T9 (Book p662)

questions.q: Once the spinal segment is localized, the next printed step is to:
opts: Assume a vertebral level equal to the dermatome
Localize compression to the corresponding vertebral segment
questions.exp: Once spinal segment is localized : Localize compression to corresponding vertebral segment (Book p662)

questions.q: Which finding is given the best localizing value?
questions.exp: Reflex level : Best localizing value (Book p662)

questions.q: The printed procedure for eliciting Beevor's sign is to:
opts: Ask the patient to get up from the supine position
Ask the patient to cough with feet standing
questions.exp: Beevor's sign : Procedure : Ask patient to get up from supine position (Book p662)

questions.q: The normal segmental supply of the abdominal wall is printed as:
opts: Upper T7-T9 and lower T9-T12 contracting together
questions.exp: Normal : upper (T7-T9) & lower (T9-T12) abdomen contracts together → No deviation of umbilicus (Book p662)

questions.q: On a sit-up test the patient's umbilicus is pulled upward because the lower abdominal wall is weak. Which interpretation does the book give?
opts: Beevor sign positive, implying a lesion below T9
Beevor sign negative, no cord lesion
questions.exp: weakness of lower abdomen : upper abdominal muscle contraction pull umbilicus above (Beevor sign positive) (Book p662)

questions.q: The printed direction of damage in intramedullary compression is:
questions.exp: Damage — Intramedullary : Centrifugal (Centre → Periphery of spinal cord) (Book p662)

questions.q: Pain in the extramedullary column is of which type?
questions.exp: Pain — Intramedullary : Funicular; Extramedullary : Root pain (Book p662)

questions.q: Dissociative and suspended sensory loss appear in which column?
opts: Both positive in intramedullary, both negative in extramedullary
questions.exp: Dissociative sensory loss + / − and Suspended sensory loss + / − for intramedullary vs extramedullary (Book p662)

questions.q: Sacral sparing is printed as:
opts: Present in intramedullary, absent in extramedullary
Absent in intramedullary, present in extramedullary
questions.exp: Sacral sparing — Intramedullary +; Extramedullary − (Book p662)

questions.q: Trophic changes in the table are attributed to:
opts: Posterior column loss, positive in extramedullary
Pain and temperature loss, positive in intramedullary
questions.exp: Trophic changes (D/t pain & temperature loss) — Intramedullary +; Extramedullary − (Book p662)

questions.q: Pyramidal (UMN) signs appear in which temporal pattern?
opts: Late in intramedullary, early in extramedullary
Early in intramedullary, late in extramedullary
questions.exp: Pyramidal signs (UMN) — Intramedullary : Late; Extramedullary : Early (Book p662)

questions.q: LMN signs follow which pattern in the table?
opts: Early in intramedullary, late in extramedullary
Late in intramedullary, early in extramedullary
questions.exp: LMN signs — Intramedullary : Early; Extramedullary : Late (Book p662)

questions.q: Bowel and bladder involvement is printed as:
opts: Early in intramedullary, late in extramedullary
Late in intramedullary, early in extramedullary
questions.exp: Bowel/bladder — Intramedullary : Early; Extramedullary : Late (Book p662)

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of extramedullary rather than intramedullary compression?
questions.exp: Spinal deformity — Intramedullary −; Extramedullary + (Book p662)

questions.q: A young woman has 2 years of cape-like dissociated loss with sacral sparing, early bladder symptoms and only mild pyramidal signs. Which mechanism does the printed comparison imply?
opts: Centrifugal intramedullary damage from the central cord outward
Centripetal extramedullary compression of the surface tracts
questions.exp: Intramedullary : Centrifugal damage, dissociative and suspended sensory loss +, sacral sparing +, bowel/bladder early, pyramidal signs late (Book p662)

questions.q: The two fasciculi labelled in the posterior columns of the cross-section are:
opts: Anterior and posterior external arcuate fibres
Medial lemniscus and external cuneate nucleus
questions.exp: Figure labels : Fasciculus cuneatus; Fasciculus gracilis (Book p663)

questions.q: The bracket joining lateral corticospinal (pyramidal) and rubrospinal tracts assigns which action?
questions.exp: Lateral corticospinal (pyramidal) tract + Rubrospinal tract → Distal limb movements (Book p663)

questions.q: Lateral reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal and tectospinal tracts are grouped for:
questions.exp: Figure bracket : Lateral reticulospinal; Vestibulospinal; Ventral reticulospinal; Tectospinal → Axial and proximal limb movements (Book p663)

questions.q: Which structure is NOT labelled on this mid-thoracic cross-section figure?
questions.exp: The figure labels fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis, dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts, lateral and ventral spinothalamic tracts, the anterior horn, corticospinal, rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts, not the fasciculus proprius (Book p663)

questions.q: The ventral (uncrossed) corticospinal tract is labelled with which role?
questions.exp: Ventral (uncrossed) corticospinal tract : Distal limb movements (minor role) (Book p663)

questions.q: Root pain or girdle pain is characterized as:
opts: Shooting pain only on neck flexion
Brief shock-like pain along distribution, initially unilateral then bilateral
Constant dull ache from within the cord
questions.exp: Root pain/girdle pain : Character — Brief shock like pain along distribution (initially U/L → B/L) (Book p663)

questions.q: Lhermitte sign is characterized as:
opts: Shortness of breath with neck extension
Shooting pain along spinal cord till sacrum
questions.exp: Lhermitte sign : Character — Shooting pain along spinal cord till sacrum (Book p663)

questions.q: Coughing or Valsalva aggravates which printed entity?
questions.exp: Exacerbated by — Root pain : Coughing/valsava; Lhermitte : On flexion of neck (Book p663)

questions.q: The cause given for Lhermitte sign is:
questions.exp: Cause — Lhermitte sign : Posterior compression (Extramedullary) (Book p663)

questions.q: For localization, the table prints:
opts: Root pain useful (+), Lhermitte sign not useful (−)
questions.exp: Useful for localization — Root pain +; Lhermitte sign − (Book p663)

questions.q: Funicular or tract pain is described as:
opts: Brief electric shocks on neck flexion
Constant, dull, aching pain from within
questions.exp: Funicular pain/tract pain : Constant, dull, aching pain from within (Book p663)

questions.q: Suspended sensory loss is explained by:
opts: Loss of crossing over ST tract fibres at the level
Complete transection of the spinothalamic tract
questions.exp: Suspended sensory loss : D/t loss of crossing over ST tract fibres at the level (Book p663)

questions.q: In suspended sensory loss, the sensation above and below the involved level is:
opts: Also lost in a stocking pattern
questions.exp: Above and below level of involvement : Normal (Book p663)

questions.q: Dissociative sensory loss means:
opts: Loss of spinothalamic sensation with intact posterior column
Loss of posterior column with intact pain sensation
questions.exp: Dissociative sensory loss : Loss of spinothalamic tract sensation with intact posterior column (Book p663)

questions.q: An early LMN finding in intramedullary disease occurs when the lesion reaches the:
questions.exp: Early LMN finding : when lesion reach anterior horn cell (AHC) (Book p663)

questions.q: The lamination of spinothalamic fibres from centre to periphery is printed as:
questions.exp: Spinothalamic tract fibres : Centre → Periphery : CTLS (C : cervical, T : Thoracic, L : Lumbar, S : Sacral) (Book p663)

questions.q: Bowel and bladder fibres are placed where, and with what consequence?
opts: In the posterior columns, so sensory-only bladder symptoms
In the centre, so early involvement in intramedullary disease
At the periphery, so late involvement
Only in the conus, so absent in cord disease
questions.exp: Bowel & bladder fibres are in the centre : Early involvement in intramedullary (Book p663)

questions.q: Because the corticospinal tract lies towards the periphery, intramedullary lesions give:
questions.exp: Corticospinal tract situated towards periphery : Late UMN involvement in intramedullary (Book p663)

questions.q: The mechanism printed for raised CSF protein in extramedullary disease is:
questions.exp: CSF protein : D/t root involvement (Book p663)

questions.q: A central cervical cord lesion starts producing ptosis and miosis on one side. Which printed explanation fits?
opts: Intramedullary extension damaging sympathetic fibres at the cervical level → Horner's syndrome
Compression of the trochlear nerve in its cisternal course
Pre-ganglionic T1 root avulsion from trauma
questions.exp: Intramedullary : Extension can damage sympathetic fibre in cervical level → Horner's syndrome (Book p663)

questions.q: Conus medullaris involvement is printed as affecting:
opts: B/L S3 → C1 inside the spinal cord
questions.exp: Involvement — Conus medullaris : B/L S3 → C1 inside spinal cord (printed C1 for the coccygeal segment, as in Ch50) (Book p664)

questions.q: Onset in the two columns is printed as:
opts: Sudden in conus, insidious in cauda equina
Insidious in conus, sudden in cauda equina
questions.exp: Onset — Conus : Sudden onset; Cauda equina : Insidious (Book p664)

questions.q: Root pain in the two columns is described as:
opts: Common in conus, absent in cauda equina
Uncommon in conus, unilateral in leg, thigh and bladder regions in cauda equina
questions.exp: Root pain — Conus : Uncommon; Cauda equina : U/L in leg, thigh, bladder (Book p664)

questions.q: Sensory loss patterns are:
opts: Saddle distribution in conus, saddle or any part of the lower limb in cauda equina
Stocking in conus, saddle in cauda equina only
Dissociated loss in cauda equina only
questions.exp: Sensory loss — Conus : Saddle distribution; Cauda equina : Saddle/any part of LL (Book p664)

questions.q: Motor findings in the two columns are:
opts: No weakness in conus; weakness and wasting of LL muscles in cauda equina
Wasting in conus, none in cauda equina
questions.exp: motor — Conus : No weakness; Cauda equina : weakness & wasting of LL muscles (Book p664)

questions.q: Deep tendon reflexes in conus lesions are printed as:
opts: Normal, with anal and bulbocavernous reflexes lost
Lost knee and ankle jerks always
questions.exp: Deep tendon reflex (DTR) — Conus : Normal (Anal & bulbocavernous reflexes lost) (Book p664)

questions.q: Bladder, bowel and sexual function rows read:
opts: Negative in conus, positive in cauda equina
Only bowel is involved in conus
Positive in conus for all three; negative in cauda equina for all three
questions.exp: Bladder +/−, Bowel +/− and Sexual +/− for conus versus cauda equina (Book p664)

questions.q: An elderly man has 6 months of asymmetric radicular pain, asymmetric areflexic leg weakness with wasting, saddle numbness and only late urinary symptoms. Which syndrome is printed for this pattern?
questions.exp: Cauda equina : asymmetrical L2 → C1 roots, insidious, U/L root pain, weakness & wasting of LL muscles, loss of knee & ankle jerk, bladder/bowel/sexual − (Book p664)

questions.q: The epiconus is printed as involving which segments?
questions.exp: Epiconus : Involves : L4, L5, S1, S2 (Book p664)

questions.q: In epiconus lesions, which movement is spared?
questions.exp: Lower limb weakness : Hip flexion/adduction spared (Book p664)

questions.q: Bladder involvement in epiconus lesions is printed as:
questions.exp: Bladder : UMN (Book p664)

questions.q: The mnemonic printed for non-compressive myelopathy causes is:
questions.exp: Non Compressive Myelopathy — Causes : mnemonic : VITAMIN (Book p664)

questions.q: The vascular entry under the first VITAMIN category is:
questions.exp: Vascular : Anterior spinal artery (ASA) thrombosis (Book p664)

questions.q: Which entity is NOT printed as a demyelinating cause of non-compressive myelopathy?
questions.exp: Demyelinating causes printed are multiple sclerosis (MS) and Neuromyelitis optica (NMO); sarcoid is printed separately under Autoimmune (Book p664)

questions.q: The inherited cause printed under VITAMIN is:
questions.exp: Inherited : Friedreich's ataxia (Book p664)

questions.q: The toxin entry is:
questions.exp: Toxin : Arsenic (Book p664)

questions.q: The autoimmune entry is:
questions.exp: Autoimmune : Sarcoid (Book p664)

questions.q: The metabolic entry names which disease?
questions.exp: Metabolic : Sub acute combined degeneration (Book p664)

questions.q: Subacute combined degeneration is otherwise printed as:
opts: Anterolateral cord syndrome, due to vitamin E excess
Central cord syndrome, due to folate deficiency
Posterior root radiculopathy due to vitamin B1 deficiency
Posterolateral cord syndrome, due to vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.exp: Sub acute combined degeneration : Posterolateral cord syndrome; D/t vitamin B12 deficiency (Book p664)

questions.q: Which is NOT among the printed differential diagnoses of subacute combined degeneration?
questions.exp: Differential diagnosis : Vitamin E deficiency, Copper deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1 (Book p664)

questions.q: A 34-year-old strict vegan has 1 year of numb feet, sensory ataxia and extensor plantars with macrocytic anaemia. Under which VITAMIN heading is his disease printed?
questions.exp: Metabolic : Sub acute combined degeneration — D/t vitamin B12 deficiency, aetiology also given as arsenic under Toxin but not B12 (Book p664)

questions.q: Under 'Infection' among VITAMIN causes, the two entities printed are:
opts: Lyme neuroborreliosis and HIV vacuolar myelopathy
Acute transverse myelitis as a post-infectious complication, and syphilis (tabes dorsalis) with TB
questions.exp: Infection : Acute transverse myelitis (Post infectious complication); Syphilis (Tabes dorsalis), TB (Book p665)

questions.q: Acute transverse myelitis is defined in the book as:
opts: Chronic progressive demyelination limited to one root
Suppurative infection of the epidural space
Vascular malformation of the conus with haematomyelia
Rapid onset full thickness/segmented monophasic inflammation of the spinal cord
questions.exp: ACUTE TRANSVERSE MYELITIS : Rapid onset full thickness/segmented monophasic inflammation of the spinal cord (myelitis : inflammation of cord) (Book p665)

questions.q: The second definitional line describes ATM as a demyelinating disease that:
opts: Can affect a variable number of segments
questions.exp: Demyelinating disease which can affect variable number of segments (Book p665)

questions.q: The dermatome table pairs the level of the nipples with:
questions.exp: Dermatome table : T4 Level of nipples (Book p665)

questions.q: The level of the umbilicus is printed as:
questions.exp: Dermatome table : T10 Level of umbilicus (Book p665)

questions.q: The lateral parts of the upper limbs are supplied by:
questions.exp: Dermatome table : C5,6,7 Lateral parts of upper limbs; C8, T1 Medial sides of upper limbs (Book p665)

questions.q: The thumb and the ring/little fingers are assigned to which dermatomes?
opts: C6 for the thumb, C8 for ring and little fingers
C5 for the thumb, T1 for ring and little fingers
C7 for the thumb, C8 for ring and little fingers
C6 for the thumb, T1 for ring and little fingers
questions.exp: Dermatome table : C6 Thumb; C8 Ring and little fingers (Book p665)

questions.q: Which pairing is NOT as printed in the dermatome table?
opts: L1,2,3,4 : anterior and inner surfaces of lower limbs
L5 : medial side of great toe
L4 : medial side of great toe
questions.exp: Dermatome table : L4 Medial side of great toe; L4,5, S1 Foot; L1.2.3.4 Anterior and inner surfaces of lower limbs (Book p665)

questions.q: The perineum is supplied by which dermatomes in this table?
questions.exp: Dermatome table : S2,3,4 Perineum (Book p665)

questions.q: The m/c cause printed for acute transverse myelitis is:
questions.exp: Causes : Post infectious (m/c) (Book p665)

questions.q: Which of these causes is NOT printed in the ATM list?
questions.exp: Causes : Post infectious (m/c), Vaccination, multiple sclerosis, Sarcoidosis, Paraneoplastic, Neuromyelitis optica, Bechet's disease (Book p665)

questions.q: The bracket in the ATM causes list groups the longitudinally extending transverse myelitis set, which runs from:
opts: Multiple sclerosis through Behcet's disease (MS, sarcoidosis, paraneoplastic, NMO, Behcet's)
questions.exp: Bracket over multiple sclerosis, Sarcoidosis, Paraneoplastic, Neuromyelitis optica, Bechet's disease : Longitudinally extending transverse myelitis (Book p665)

questions.q: The sensory onset of ATM is printed as:
opts: Paresthesia beginning in the feet and extending upward to the trunk
Cape-like loss starting in the hands
questions.exp: Clinical features : Paresthesia beginning in the feet and extending upward to trunk (Book p665)

questions.q: The initial back pain and paraesthesia of ATM evolve into:
questions.exp: Back pain, paraesthesia → Evolve into spastic weakness (Book p665)

questions.q: The peak of deficits in ATM is reached within:
questions.exp: Peak reached within : 4 hours to 21 days (Book p665)

questions.q: The plateau phase of ATM has which mean duration?
questions.exp: Plateau phase : mean duration 1 week (Book p665)

questions.q: The band-like constriction of ATM occurs:
opts: In a glove and stocking pattern
At the level of the definite sensory level
questions.exp: Definite sensory level : Band like constriction at the level (Book p665)

questions.q: Below the sensory level in ATM, sensation shows:
opts: Complete loss of all sensory modalities
questions.exp: Complete loss of all sensory modalities below the level (Book p665)

questions.q: A patient with half-thickness cord inflammation has ipsilateral loss of vibration and position with contralateral pain-temperature loss. How is this printed?
opts: If half thickness involvement : U/L posterior column loss + C/L spinothalamic loss
Dissociated loss confined to the arms
Sacral sparing with normal modality testing
questions.exp: If half thickness involvement : U/L posterior column loss + C/L spinothalamic loss (Book p665)

questions.q: Motor weakness in ATM is described as:
opts: Below the level of involvement, paraparesis symmetrical or asymmetrical
Above the level of involvement, monoparesis
questions.exp: motor weakness : Below the level of involvement (Paraparesis : Symmetrical/asymmetrical) (Book p665)

questions.q: Significant bowel and bladder involvement in ATM presents as:
opts: Nocturnal enuresis with normal post-void residual
questions.exp: Significant bowel/bladder involvement : urinary retention (Book p665)

questions.q: Which feature of GBS is listed to separate it from ATM?
opts: Progressive lower limb weakness, proximal greater than distal
questions.exp: GBS : Progressive lower limb weakness (Proximal > distal) (Book p666)

questions.q: Regarding sensory and bladder findings, GBS is printed as:
opts: Normal sensory examination, no band-like sensation and no bladder symptoms
Definite sensory level with urinary retention
Band-like trunk pain with brisk reflexes
Sacral sensory loss with extensor plantars
questions.exp: Normal sensory examination; No band like sensation (Definite sensory level); No bladder symptoms (Book p666)

questions.q: The sagittal MRI with a red arrow pointing to a cord hyperintensity is captioned:
questions.exp: Image annotation : Hyperintensity, caption Acute transverse myelitis (level markers C3 to T8) (Book p666)

questions.q: The investigations printed for ATM are:
opts: Spinal angiography and serum B12 only
MRI T2 of spine showing hyperintensities at the level, and CSF pleocytosis >10 cells with raised IgG index
CT myelogram with somatosensory evoked potentials
questions.exp: Investigations : MRI T2 of spine : Hyperintensities at the level; CSF : Pleocytosis (>10 cells), ↑ IgG index (Book p666)

questions.q: The printed steroid regimen for ATM is:
opts: Methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV in 100 ml NS over 1 hour
questions.exp: Treatment : High dose methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg IV in 100ml NS over 1 hour) (Book p666)

questions.q: When high-dose methylprednisolone fails in ATM, the printed next step is:
questions.exp: High dose methylprednisolone — No response → Plasma exchange (Book p666)

questions.q: Which is NOT among the printed indications for plasma exchange?
questions.exp: Indications for plasma exchange : Inability to walk; markedly impaired autonomic function; Sensory loss in lower extremities; No/little improvement after 5-7 days of IV steroids (Book p666)

questions.q: Subacute combined degeneration is printed as an abbreviation of:
opts: Central cord syndrome of periventricular white matter
Combined systems atrophy of the basal ganglia
Posterolateral cord syndrome of the white matter
Anterolateral cord syndrome of grey matter
questions.exp: SUBACUTE COMBINED DEGENERATION (SACD) : AKA posterolateral cord syndrome (white matter); D/t vitamin B12 deficiency (Book p666)

questions.q: The first tract involved in the printed progression is:
opts: Posterior tract, with posterior column sensations lost
questions.exp: Progression of disease : Posterior tract : Posterior column sensations lost (Book p666)

questions.q: The first symptom and first sign of SCD are printed respectively as:
opts: Tingling and paraesthesia of the distal extremity; vibration sense lost first
questions.exp: Tingling, paraesthesia of distal extremity : First symptom; Vibration sense lost first : First sign (Book p666)

questions.q: After the posterior column, which pair of sensations is printed as lost next?
opts: Two-point discrimination of the palms only
questions.exp: Fine touch and proprioception lost; then sensory ataxia, gait abnormality (Book p666)

questions.q: The lateral-tract step of the flowchart includes which two tracts?
questions.exp: Lateral tract : Spinothalamic tract; Corticospinal tract (Book p666)

questions.q: The final arrow of the progression adds which peripheral finding?
opts: Large fibre neuropathy with reflexes lost and glove and stocking neuropathy
questions.exp: Large fibre neuropathy : Reflex lost (knee jerk, ankle jerk), glove & stocking neuropathy (Book p666)

questions.q: If SCD is left untreated, the complication arrow lists dementia and which other feature?
questions.exp: If not treated — Complication → Dementia, optic atrophy (Book p666)

questions.q: Friedreich's ataxia is introduced as:
questions.exp: FRIEDREICH'S ATAXIA : Commonest form of spinocerebellar degeneration (Book p667)

questions.q: The cerebellum itself in Friedreich's ataxia is:
questions.exp: Cerebellum is normal (Book p667)

questions.q: The inheritance rows are printed as:
opts: Autosomal recessive more common with early onset, autosomal dominant with later onset
questions.exp: Inheritance : Autosomal recessive : more common, early onset (8-20 yrs); Autosomal dominant : Later onset (Book p667)

questions.q: The early-onset age window printed for the autosomal-recessive form is:
questions.exp: Autosomal recessive : more common, early onset (8-20 yrs) (Book p667)

questions.q: The gene defect printed for Friedreich's ataxia is:
opts: FRATAXIN on chromosome 9 with GAA repetition
questions.exp: Gene defect : FRATAXIN (Chr 9) : GAA repetition (Book p667)

questions.q: Which two structures are explicitly printed as spared in Friedreich's ataxia?
questions.exp: Cerebrum & cranial nerve spared (Book p667)

questions.q: The printed order of involvement in Friedreich's ataxia is:
opts: Dorsal root ganglion → spinocerebellar tract → cord → lastly nerve
questions.exp: Involvement : DSC : Dorsal root ganglion → Spinocerebellar tract → Cord → Lastly nerve (Book p667)

questions.q: DRG involvement produces which printed feature?
questions.exp: DRG : Severe sensory ataxia (Book p667)

questions.q: Cord involvement in Friedreich's ataxia affects which columns, and gives what?
opts: Posterior and lateral columns → UMN findings with extensor plantar
Anterior and posterior columns → LMN findings
Only lateral spinothalamic tract → suspended sensory loss
questions.exp: Cord : Posterior and lateral columns → UMN findings (Extensor plantar) (Book p667)

questions.q: The peripheral-nerve row lists neuropathy with which two features?
questions.exp: Peripheral nerves : Neuropathy → Reflexes lost; Demyelination (Book p667)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT in the printed non-neurological list for Friedreich's ataxia?
opts: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy with systemic hypertension
questions.exp: Non neurological manifestations : Scoliosis, Cardiac symptoms (myocardial fibrosis in 90%, cardiomyopathy), Diabetic mellitus, Optic atrophy, Deafness, Pes cavus, Hammer toe (Book p667)

questions.q: Myocardial fibrosis in Friedreich's ataxia is printed as occurring in:
questions.exp: Cardiac symptoms : myocardial fibrosis in 90%, cardiomyopathy (Book p667)

questions.q: Tabes dorsalis is introduced as a manifestation of:
questions.exp: TABES DORSALIS : manifestation of neurosyphilis (Book p667)

questions.q: Which is NOT among the printed tabes dorsalis involvement rows?
opts: Severe radicular pain from nerve root involvement
questions.exp: Involvement : DRG : Sensory ataxia; Bowel and bladder involvement; Nerve root : Severe radicular pain, Loss of reflexes, Absent plantar response (Book p667)

units.title: 1. Myelopathy Definition and the Compressive Compartments
units.guide:
Myelopathy is printed as sensory, motor or ANS symptoms d/t disease of spinal cord, divided into compressive and non-compressive; compressive myelopathy runs a chronic course.
The type table splits compressive myelopathy into intramedullary versus extramedullary, and extramedullary into intradural versus extradural, with extradural marked m/c.
Intramedullary = tumours (ependymoma, oligodendroglioma, medulloblastoma) plus expansion of cavity (syringomyelia); intradural = neurofibroma, meningioma, arachnoid cyst, pachymeningitis; extradural = vertebral lesions (fracture, TB/syphilis, pyogenic abscess, prostate & ovary metastasis), IVDP (m/c) and aneurysm of aorta.

units.title: 2. Clinical Features, Claudication Table and Examination
units.guide:
Chronic back pain is moderate to severe, worse on erect posture (canal diameter ↓ in standing) and relieved on bending or cycling; with band-like hyperesthesia at the involved level (umbilicus if T10), these are printed as definitive symptoms of compression.
The note table separates neurogenic claudication (variable distance, relieved by sitting/bending, painless uphill, bicycle test negative, pulses present, back pain common, numbness proximal→distal) from vascular claudication (fixed distance, relieved by standing, painful uphill, bicycle test positive, pulses absent, cramping distal→proximal).
Examination shows normal HMF and cranial nerves, intact upper-limb power and sensation with compression below T1, reduced lower-limb power with B/L UMN features, spinothalamic plus posterior-column loss, exaggerated knee and ankle jerks, extensor plantars, and bowel-bladder involvement in intramedullary compression.

units.title: 3. Level Localization and the Beevor Procedure
units.guide:
LMN findings, wasting, band-like sensation, hyperesthesia, hypesthesia and hypoalgesia localise at the level of lesion, while UMN findings with lost superficial and exaggerated deep reflexes sit below it; upper limbs normal means the lesion is below T1, with everything above spared.
Sensory symptoms plus weakness in both legs place the lesion above L1; a positive Beevor's sign indicates a lesion below T9; once the spinal segment is found, the compression is localized to the corresponding vertebral segment, and the reflex level carries the best localizing value.
Beevor's sign: ask the patient to rise from supine; normally upper (T7-T9) and lower (T9-T12) abdomen contract together with no umbilical deviation, whereas lower-abdominal weakness lets the upper muscles pull the umbilicus upward, which is a positive sign.

units.title: 4. The Centrifugal-Centripetal Comparison Table
units.guide:
Intramedullary damage runs centrifugal from centre to periphery; extramedullary damage runs centripetal from periphery to centre, so pain is funicular inside the cord and root pain outside it.
The table marks dissociative sensory loss, suspended sensory loss, sacral sparing and trophic changes as intramedullary positives; pyramidal signs are late intramedullary but early extramedullary, LMN signs and bowel-bladder involvement early intramedullary but late extramedullary, while spinal deformity, spinal tenderness and raised CSF protein favour the extramedullary side.

units.title: 5. Tract Layout, Root Pain versus Lhermitte Sign and the Intramedullary Logic
units.guide:
The mid-thoracic cross-section labels fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis (CTLS from lateral to medial), dorsal and ventral roots, dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts, lateral spinothalamic (pain, temperature) and ventral spinothalamic (pressure, touch), ventral uncrossed corticospinal (distal limb, minor role), anterior horn motor neurons, and the lateral corticospinal plus rubrospinal tracts for distal limb movements with reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts for axial and proximal limb movements.
Root or girdle pain is brief, shock-like, initially unilateral then bilateral, provoked by coughing or Valsalva, caused by posterolateral compression and useful for localization; Lhermitte sign is shooting pain down the cord to the sacrum on neck flexion from posterior extramedullary compression but is not useful for localization.
Funicular pain is constant and dull from within; suspended sensory loss reflects loss of crossing spinothalamic fibres at the level with normal sensation above and below; CTLS lamination explains sacral sparing, central bladder fibres explain early sphincter involvement, peripheral corticospinal tracts explain late UMN signs, raised CSF protein reflects root involvement, and cervical intramedullary extension can interrupt sympathetics to give Horner's syndrome.

units.title: 6. Conus versus Cauda Equina, Epiconus and the VITAMIN Causes
units.guide:
Conus medullaris involvement is printed as B/L S3-C1 inside the spinal cord with sudden onset, uncommon root pain, saddle sensory loss, dissociated sensory loss, no weakness, normal knee and ankle jerks with lost anal and bulbocavernous reflexes, and early bladder, bowel and sexual involvement; cauda equina is asymmetrical L2-C1 roots with insidious onset, unilateral root pain in leg, thigh and bladder, saddle or any-leg sensory loss, weakness and wasting of leg muscles, lost knee and ankle jerks, and later sphincter involvement.
Epiconus involves L4, L5, S1 and S2 with hip flexion and adduction spared, thigh sensation spared, both knee and ankle jerks lost and an UMN-type bladder.
Non-compressive myelopathy causes run on the VITAMIN mnemonic: vascular (ASA thrombosis) and demyelinating (MS, NMO), inherited Friedreich's ataxia, arsenic toxin, sarcoid autoimmunity, metabolic subacute combined degeneration, infection and neoplasia.

units.title: 7. Dermatomes, Causes and Clinical Features of ATM
units.guide:
Infection and neoplasia close the VITAMIN list: acute transverse myelitis as a post-infectious complication and syphilis or TB among the infections.
Acute transverse myelitis is printed as rapid-onset full-thickness or segmented monophasic inflammation of the spinal cord, a demyelinating disease that can affect a variable number of segments; the dermatome table runs from C5 (clavicles) and C6 (thumb) through C8 (ring and little fingers), T4 (nipples), T10 (umbilicus), T12 (groin), L1-L4 anterior and inner leg, L4 great toe, L4-L5-S1 foot, S1 outer foot and little toe and S2-S4 perineum.
Causes are post-infectious (m/c), vaccination, MS, sarcoidosis, paraneoplastic, neuromyelitis optica and Behcet's disease, the last four bracketed as longitudinally extending transverse myelitis; features are ascending paresthesia from the feet, back pain evolving into spastic weakness, peak within 4 hours to 21 days, a plateau of about a week, a definite sensory level with band-like constriction, complete loss below it, half-cord patterns, symmetrical or asymmetrical paraparesis, prominent sphincter involvement with urinary retention and brisk reflexes below the level.

units.title: 8. Differentiating ATM from GBS, Investigations, Treatment and Combined Degeneration
units.guide:
GBS is separated from ATM by progressive lower-limb weakness that is proximal greater than distal, ascending paralysis, areflexia, a normal sensory examination, absence of a band-like definite sensory level and absence of bladder symptoms.
Work-up is MRI T2 of the spine showing hyperintensities at the level, with CSF pleocytosis above 10 cells and a raised IgG index; treatment is high-dose methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV in 100 ml NS over 1 hour, escalating to plasma exchange when there is no response, the exchange indications being inability to walk, markedly impaired autonomic function, sensory loss in the lower extremities and no or little improvement after 5-7 days of IV steroids.
Subacute combined degeneration is printed as posterolateral cord syndrome from B12 deficiency, progressing from posterior-column first symptom of distal tingling and first sign of lost vibration, to lateral-tract spinothalamic and corticospinal involvement with extensor plantars, then large-fibre neuropathy with lost reflexes and glove-and-stocking changes, and, if untreated, dementia and optic atrophy.

units.title: 9. Friedreich's Ataxia and Tabes Dorsalis
units.guide:
Friedreich's ataxia is printed as the commonest spinocerebellar degeneration with a normal cerebellum, FRATAXIN gene defect on chromosome 9 with GAA repetition, autosomal-recessive early onset between 8 and 20 years and a later-onset autosomal-dominant form, cerebrum and cranial nerves spared, males greater than females, and sagittal MRI showing a normal cerebellum while ataxia-telangiectasia shows an atrophic one.
Involvement runs dorsally from root ganglion to spinocerebellar tract, cord and finally nerve: severe sensory ataxia, cerebellar ataxia with horizontal nystagmus and dysarthria, extensor plantars from posterior and lateral columns, then reflexes lost from demyelinating neuropathy, with scoliosis, myocardial fibrosis in 90%, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, optic atrophy, deafness, pes cavus and hammer toe.
Tabes dorsalis, a neurosyphilis manifestation, gives DRG sensory ataxia with bowel and bladder involvement plus root pain, lost reflexes and absent plantar responses.
